clinicalPearls: A benign congenital foregut duplication cyst lined by respiratory epithelium, usually located in the mediastinum near the carina or within the lung
Many are asymptomatic and found incidentally on chest imaging
Symptoms, when present, arise from mass effect on the airway or oesophagus, causing cough, wheeze, stridor, or dysphagia, and from secondary infection
Classically appears as a well-defined, thin-walled, homogeneous mass of fluid density that does not enhance
High protein or mucoid content can raise the apparent density on CT and mimic a solid lesion, where MRI helps confirm fluid nature
Complications include infection, haemorrhage into the cyst, and rarely fistulation or airway compression
Complete surgical excision is generally recommended to confirm the diagnosis, relieve symptoms, and prevent complications
reference.pathophysiology: Bronchogenic cysts result from abnormal budding of the ventral foregut, the primitive tracheobronchial tree, during early embryonic development. A group of cells becomes separated from the developing airway and forms a closed cyst lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium, often with cartilage, smooth muscle, and mucous glands in its wall. The cyst fills with clear or mucoid secretion and enlarges slowly. Because it does not communicate with the airway it usually remains sterile, but a connection or bacterial seeding can lead to infection, and expansion may compress the trachea, bronchi, or oesophagus.
additionalDifferentials: Neurogenic tumour in the posterior mediastinum
Necrotic lymph node or abscess when infected
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax to define location, wall, and fluid density
MRI to confirm the cystic nature of high-density lesions
Bronchoscopy or endoscopic ultrasound where airway or oesophageal involvement is suspected
Barium swallow if oesophageal compression causes dysphagia
Surgical excision with histology for definitive diagnosis
redFlags: Acute airway compromise or stridor from tracheobronchial compression
Signs of infection or abscess formation within the cyst
Rapid enlargement or haemorrhage into the cyst
reference.prognosis: Bronchogenic cysts are benign, and complete excision is curative with an excellent long-term outlook; untreated cysts may enlarge or become infected, and malignant change is very rare.
pitfalls: Mistaking a high-density mucoid cyst on CT for a solid tumour and missing the diagnosis
Attributing symptoms to another cause when a cyst is compressing the airway or oesophagus
Assuming an incidental cyst is always safe to leave when complications or diagnostic uncertainty exist
Incomplete excision leaving epithelial remnants that predispose to recurrence
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Offer complete surgical excision, thoracoscopic or open, which is curative and prevents infection, haemorrhage, and compression
Treat secondary infection with antibiotics, and drain where needed, before definitive resection
Consider excision even in asymptomatic cysts given the risk of enlargement and complications, or interval imaging surveillance if surgery is deferred
Confirm the cystic nature with MRI for high-density lesions and obtain histology to exclude rare malignancy
Relieve significant airway or oesophageal compression, with endoscopic or image-guided aspiration in selected unfit patients
Refer to a thoracic surgical team for definitive management
